sections: Gmail and Outlook limit attachments to about 20–25 MB in total. If your ZIP is bigger, compress the content first – [Compress PDF](/compress-pdf/), [Compress Image](/compress-image/), [Compress Video](/compress-video/) – or share through cloud storage.

Give files clear names before zipping – *2026-10-invoice-acme.pdf* is far more useful to the recipient than *scan0042.pdf*. Put a short README.txt in the ZIP when sending many files to explain what is inside. Avoid characters such as / \ : * ? " < > | in names, which Windows cannot use. If you will send the ZIP again later, include the date in its name so versions are easy to tell apart.

The ZIP is standard and opens natively on Windows (Extract All), macOS (double-click), Linux, Android and iOS Files. File names with accents and non-Latin scripts are stored in UTF-8. For better compression of large archives consider 7Z via [Create TAR.GZ](/create-tar-gz/) options.

No WinRAR, 7-Zip or app needed: it runs in Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on Windows, macOS, Linux, ChromeOS, Android and iPhone. On iPhone and iPad, extracted files go to the Files app; on Android, to Downloads. Large archives are limited only by your device's memory – a few gigabytes on a laptop, less on phones.

list: Only open archives from people and sites you trust; extracting a file is safe, but running an unknown .exe, .bat or .js inside it is not.
Watch for double extensions such as invoice.pdf.exe.
Scan downloaded executables with your antivirus before running them.
Password-protected archives from unknown senders are a common way to slip malware past e-mail filters – be careful.

sections: A ZIP file is a container that holds one or more files and folders, each compressed individually with the Deflate algorithm. Because each file is stored separately, a ZIP can be opened and a single file extracted quickly without reading the whole archive.
